title: Onprem airgapped runtime + KV batching + offline licensing deep dive

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-20 15:00 UTC
Duration: 1:15:00 (approx)
Location: Zoom
Recording: yes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (CTO, Atlas Health), Liam O'Connor (DevOps), Dr. Sara Kim (AI/ML Lead)
Shared artifacts: onboarding deck (link), security pack placeholder, benchmark spreadsheet (link)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for carving out time today, uh this is the deep dive we promised on the onprem / airgapped flow, i'll let priya drive most of the tech but i'll jump in for licensing and SOW stuff.
[00:18] Maya: thanks jordan, appreciate it, we really need to validate performance on our infra before we sign off for PHI workloads.
[00:30] Priya: cool, quick agenda: runtime perf, kv cache behavior, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs, artifact delivery + offline licensing, driver packaging and install steps. then Q&A and next steps.
[00:52] Liam: sounds good, we have a tight maintenance window so offline bundle + clear install steps are critical.
[01:10] Jordan: noted. also quick clarifier — are you leaning Dedicated reserved capacity or full Private (on-prem) deployment?
[01:25] Maya: Private on-prem. regulatory reasons. dedicated in-cloud won't work for our PHI.
[01:35] Priya: ok perfect, that sets the constraints. we'll talk about network egress restrictions and how artifact delivery works air-gapped.

[03:12] Priya: runtime first — our serving runtime uses continuous batching and an adaptive kernel selector. in airgapped mode it's the same runtime but we ship an offline artifact bundle: model binaries, runtime, python shim, and an installer. the key bits for perf are kv cache locality, batch sizing heuristics, and quantization profile.
[04:05] Dr. Kim: you mentioned kv cache locality — can you explain how cache warmup works in a cold start scenario? we saw big perf hits last time.
[04:20] Priya: yeah so by default we do a prefix KV caching approach: when your session is interactive we keep key/value cache in GPU memory across calls for the same conversation id. cold start is expensive because the cache is empty; we recommend priming with a short warmup (100-200 tokens) or preloading a set of representative prefixes during boot — that's what the verification script will do. also we have a persistent disk-backed KV snapshot option for longer running agents.
[05:15] Liam: disk-backed snapshot — does that require a specific filesystem or do you ship an LMDB?
[05:28] Priya: we ship a small LMDB-based snapshot by default, and it's packaged in the artifact. you'll need a POSIX-ish FS, ext4 or XFS is fine. we also support network-mounted volumes but with a perf penalty — not recommended for low latency SLOs.

[07:02] Jordan: latency vs throughput question — do you have default batch windows or do we configure based on percentiles?
[07:12] Priya: both. by default the runtime adapts: it has a target P50 latency threshold and will batch up to N tokens or M requests within a 20ms microwindow. but in airgapped/private installs we let customers set explicit batch targets e.g., max_batch=8 and max_latency_ms=30. we can also pin optimization profiles per route.
[07:45] Dr. Kim: interesting, can we fix quantization profiles per model so accuracy regressions are controlled?
[07:54] Priya: yes — quantization profiles are part of the model package metadata. you can pick per-model: fp16, int8-qat, int8-static. we ship recommended profiles from our testing harness and also provide an evaluate script so you can run your prompts and get quality diffs.

[09:30] Maya: what's the expected throughput delta between fp16 and int8 for our Llama-like family?
[09:40] Priya: ballpark, on the same GPU and config, int8_static gives ~1.8-2.2x throughput vs fp16 and about 5-10% drop in some hallucination-sensitive prompts — depends on the prompt set. that's why we run evals ahead of rollouts.
[10:05] Liam: and memory usage?
[10:10] Priya: int8 roughly halves activation memory in many paths — better KV cache fit, means fewer host-GPU copies. that helps with throughput and reduces OOMs for long-context.

[12:00] Jordan: offline licensing — jordan jumps in — we provide time-bound license keys for private installs. we can do node-locked or fleet-locked licenses. node-locked maps to a hw fingerprint; fleet-locked ties to a local license server you run in the airgapped network.
[12:22] Maya: fleet-locked local license server sounds safer for us. how does renewal work offline? we can't hit an external CA easily.
[12:35] Jordan: we have an offline renewal flow: you generate a CSR on your local license server, we sign it and provide a signed token bundle via secure transfer (SFTP or on-us USB courier), then you install. the process is documented and we've done it with other healthcare customers.
[13:02] Dr. Kim: any automated telemetry capabilities? we can't send usage off-network.
[13:12] Jordan: telemetry is optional. for Private we can run in fully offline mode — no telemetry. for customers who want visibility, we support an encrypted offline log export that you push via secure handoff (SFTP) to Redwood for analysis. no automatic outbound.

[15:00] Priya: artifact delivery — two options: full installer bundle (recommended for smaller teams) or container images plus offline loader. full bundle is a tar.gz with runtime, models, drivers, and installer script. containers are OCI images exported to tar and we provide a loader that reimports. container approach is better for containerized infra but requires an image registry import step.
[15:40] Liam: driver packaging — we run on NVIDIA A40 and H100 in test; how do you handle GPU driver dependencies in airgapped installs?
[15:50] Priya: we include a driver compatibility matrix and ship driver installer binaries where redistributable is allowed. for enterprise, often customers already have driver ISOs; we provide a shim that installs CUDA, cuDNN and our runtime in the right order. for H100 there are specific kernel modules and driver minimums — we'll ask you to confirm kernel versions.
[16:20] Liam: kernel versions, great, we'll pull that. do you require specific NCCL versions for multi-GPU?
[16:30] Priya: yes we recommend NCCL 2.18+ for best perf; our multi-GPU scheduler also expects RDMA or NVLINK topology for low-latency allreduce. we can run a step-by-step checklist.

[18:12] Dr. Kim: can you talk about the benchmark plan — what inputs do you need from us?
[18:22] Priya: we'll need representative prompt sets, target latency SLOs, GPU SKU list, expected QPS and expected concurrency per user/session. ideally a sample dataset to run our eval harness.
[18:40] Jordan: we'll also instrument a simple perf test harness that runs on your infra and outputs token/sec, p50/p95/p99 latencies, and memory traces.

[20:10] Maya: about the eval harness — does it measure quality regressions automatically when switching quant profiles?
[20:18] Priya: yes we have a quality check that runs your prompt set and computes BLEU/ROUGE-ish metrics plus semantic similarity and a small human-in-the-loop diff. it flags prompts with >=X% delta and produces a report. note transcription or model name noise might show small changes; we include per-prompt annotations.

[22:00] Liam: edge case: if we have sequential multi-turn conversations with very long contexts, how do you avoid KV overflow?
[22:12] Priya: two strategies: rolling eviction policy (LRU-ish) and pinned prefixes. for very long contexts we recommend prefix compaction (summarize earlier context into a smaller embedding + keep recent tokens in kv). we can ship a compaction helper as part of the artifact.

[25:05] Priya: ops question — what's your patch window and how often will you want to update models?
[25:12] Maya: quarterly at minimum, security windows monthly for kernel patches. model updates probably quarterly.
[25:20] Priya: ok we can do a model bump process that is staged: internal testing, canary on a subset of nodes, then fleet rollout. for airgapped we'd give you the artifact bundle to import into a staging registry first.

[28:00] Jordan: license invoice/timing?
[28:08] Jordan: usual is a one-time platform fee for Private plus annual support/license. for the pilot we can do a time-limited evaluation license — tied to your license server. pricing details in the SOW we'll send.

[30:30] Dr. Kim: security stuff — do you support SAML SSO for the console and RBAC?
[30:38] Jordan: yes SAML and OIDC are supported for the console. RBAC is role-based and we provide audit logs that can be exported. again audit logs are local in airgapped by default.

[33:00] Priya: quick note on memory/perf tuning: the runtime exposes knobs: kv_memory_target, batch_window_ms, max_batch, kernel_sel_profile. adjusting kv_memory_target to fit your GPU can reduce host-GPU copies by ~20% in our tests. we usually recommend increasing batch_window_ms slightly if you can tolerate p50 bump to improve overall throughput.

[35:20] Maya: can you share a sample of those knobs and recommended defaults per GPU class?
[35:28] Priya: yes we'll include a tuning guide. defaults: A40 -> max_batch 6, kv_memory_target 8GB; H100 -> max_batch 12, kv_memory_target 16GB, int8 profile recommended for throughput testing. we'll provide the exact config file as part of the artifact.

[38:10] Liam: what about fallback policies? if a node is OOMing mid-request, can we fallback to a smaller model automatically?
[38:22] Priya: we have a graceful degradation policy — on OOM the request is retried to a fallback route if configured (e.g., a smaller quantized variant). this requires pre-deploying fallback models and routing rules in the config. we can demo that in the pilot.

[41:00] Jordan: open Qs from your side?
[41:10] Maya: last one — artifact delivery chain. you said SFTP or courier; what about sealed USB courier, do you have an attestation process?
[41:25] Jordan: we support courier in sealed, signed containers. we provide checksums and a signed manifest you verify with our public GPG key. for high-assurance installs we can do an on-site handoff and verification checklist.

[44:00] Dr. Kim: any gotchas with CUDA versions and driver modules we should watch for?
[44:10] Priya: yes kernel ABI mismatches are the biggest risk. ensure your kernel is compatible with the driver version; we list supported kernels per driver in the compatibility matrix. also watch for proprietary distro packaging differences (RHEL vs Ubuntu).

[47:30] Priya: demo-ish — running through a sample local-run: start license server (offline), import artifacts, run verification script which primes KV with sample prefixes, run perf harness. output is a CSV + JSON report.
[48:05] Liam: can verification script run as unprivileged?
[48:12] Priya: yes mostly, but driver install requires root. verification/perf is unprivileged aside from reading device nodes.

[51:00] Jordan: i'll recap next steps quickly.
[51:05] Jordan: 1) priya will share artifact checklist + driver packaging notes (due 2026-12-27). 2) i'll send security/compliance pack + SOW/pricing (due 2026-12-28). 3) atlas to send GPU sku list and topology (due 2026-12-23). 4) we target a 2-day benchmark in week of 2027-01-10.

[53:22] Maya: sounds good. one more — do you have references of other healthcare customers who've done offline installs?
[53:35] Jordan: yes we do, we'll include anonymized references and a short case study in the pack.

[55:10] Dr. Kim: ok excited to run this. any performance expectations we should set internally?
[55:20] Priya: expect P50 in tens of ms for inference on H100 for small prompts, p95 depends on batch and concurrency. we'll give a baseline from our internal tests.

[58:00] Liam: i'll follow up with kernel and driver inventory.
[58:10] Jordan: perfect.

[60:00] -- end of structured discussion --

[60:10] Quick clarifications/crosstalk:
[60:12] Maya: are there any updates on SOC2 type II?
[60:18] Jordan: Redwood is SOC2 Type II certified; full artifacts in the pack.
[60:22] Liam: can we set the installer to be idempotent for re-runs during staging?
[60:30] Priya: yes installer is idempotent, has dry-run mode.

[63:00] Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll send the packet.
[63:05] Maya: thanks both.
[63:08] Dr. Kim: thanks.
[63:10] Liam: bye.

[75:00] Meeting ended.
